strengths: Novel and useful framing: the paper systematically connects model multiplicity (Rashomon sets) to trustworthy-ML properties (robustness, stability, information leakage), positioning the Rashomon set itself as a policy/governance object — a genuinely under-explored perspective relative to prior work on fairness/sparsity within Rashomon sets.

The central robustness–privacy trade-off is illustrated both theoretically and empirically (Figure 1, Figure 5), and the two-sided 'resource vs. risk' narrative is coherent and consistently carried through the paper.

The distinction between distributional leakage (Theorem 6) and membership privacy (Theorem 5) is handled carefully and honestly; the authors explicitly note that distributional leakage does not automatically imply membership-inference risk.

Empirical verification is reasonably broad: six datasets (Adult, Bank, COMPAS, Credit, Diabetes, FICO), exact Rashomon sets via TreeFARMS, established attack tools (Kantchelian evasion, DRAFT reconstruction), five-fold aggregation, and dedicated empirical checks of Theorems 5 and 6 (Appendix C.4, C.5).

The results are presented as 'illustrative rather than exhaustive' and several limitations (e.g., low Spearman correlations on Adult/Bank, dataset-dependence of the sweet-spot regime) are discussed candidly rather than hidden.
weaknesses: Theoretical depth is limited. Most results formalize fairly obvious intuitions with elementary arguments: Theorem 1 is a counting/entropy bound (I(f;S) ≤ H(f) = log|F|), Eq. (1) is a direct triangle inequality, Theorem 4 is Pinsker's inequality, Theorem 5 is a K/n loss-perturbation argument, and Theorem 6 is a variance-of-sample-mean calculation. Correct, but none is technically demanding.

The reactive-robustness claim is evaluated only against attacks targeted at the optimal tree. If the Rashomon set (or many of its members) is actually released — the very scenario the paper's governance framing posits — a white-box adaptive attacker sees all released models and can craft perturbations that transfer across the set. The paper does not evaluate this adaptive attack, so the headline 'attacks do not transfer' conclusion is weaker than claimed.

Some theoretical statements rely on unrealistic regimes: Corollary 2 requires η → ∞ for models of larger angle to dominate, and Theorem 9's own title concedes it 'is not helpful' (the Cantelli bound becomes vacuous as k grows); its contribution to the paper is marginal.

Privacy experiments are on aggressively subsampled data (100 training points), following the DRAFT setup, which inflates reconstruction-attack success and weakens external validity for realistic deployment sizes. The proxy measure (reconstruction error) is also a somewhat indirect stand-in for the mutual-information analysis developed in theory.

Empirical support is uneven: Spearman correlations between diversity and adversarial robustness are only 0.23 (Adult) and 0.33 (Bank), with ad hoc explanations ('limited diversity ... caused by the data distributions'), showing the phenomenon is dataset-dependent.

No explicit limitations section or code/artifact availability statement; reproducibility depends on the appendix setup descriptions, and no commitment to releasing the TreeFARMS/DRAFT experimental pipelines is made.

Presentation issues: minor typographical problems (e.g., 'It's also viewed'), and Figure 15's axis label ('Accuracy - Adversarial Accuracy') combined with the text's 'drop in accuracy of at least 60%' is confusing about what is actually plotted.

strengths: The paper asks an interesting and underexplored question: how model multiplicity (Rashomon sets) affects robustness, stability, and privacy simultaneously, rather than treating these properties in isolation.

The framing of the Rashomon set as a practical 'policy object' that institutions already produce via hyperparameter sweeps, seeds, and model search is a genuinely useful governance-oriented perspective.

The empirical work is reasonably broad (six tabular datasets, TreeFARMS Rashomon sets, DRAFT-based reconstruction attacks, Kantchelian-style evasion attacks), and includes empirical verification of two theoretical claims (set stability under dataset perturbations, Theorem 5 / Figure 10; KL leakage vs. ensemble size, Theorem 6 / Figure 2).

The paper is honest in distinguishing distributional leakage from membership privacy, and the writing is generally clear, with an explicit statement that results are 'illustrative rather than exhaustive.'

The robustness mechanism (non-transferability of attacks to prediction-diverse models, Eq. 1 and Theorem 3) is correctly identified and matches the empirical correlation between Hamming distance to the optimal tree and adversarial score.
weaknesses: The central 'trade-off' framing is weaker than claimed. The robustness benefit (reactive robustness) concerns an institution that *retains* a diverse set internally and switches models, while the privacy cost arises only when models are *disclosed*. These are different operational regimes, so the paper does not establish a true unavoidable trade-off; the conclusion itself concedes this ('retain a diverse Rashomon set internally... while limiting external disclosure'), which largely dissolves the headline duality.

Several theorems are technically shallow: Theorem 1 is a counting bound I(f;S) ≤ H(f) ≤ log|F|; Theorem 4 is a direct application of Pinsker's inequality to a bounded loss; Theorem 5 is a two-line argument; Theorems 8–9 are standard Chernoff/Cantelli applications; Theorem 6 is a chi-squared upper bound on KL. Individually acceptable as illustrations, but collectively the theoretical contribution is limited, and the paper sometimes presents these as 'characterizing' the trade-off when they mostly restate known tools.

There is a theory–practice mismatch: Theorem 6 assumes models output probabilities in [δ, 1−δ], whereas the experiments release hard-classification sparse trees; the DRAFT reconstruction attack was designed for random forests and its adaptation to Rashomon sets of trees is not validated; the reconstruction experiments use only 100 training points, so it is unclear the leakage findings transfer to realistic dataset sizes.

The adversarial threat model is narrow: attacks always target only the optimal tree (white-box, single perturbation budget η=1 or η=0.1), and 'adversarial accuracy' of ~0.5–0.7 is reported without comparison to natural accuracy or to any defense baseline, making the practical significance of 'reactive robustness' hard to judge. The claim that a diverse Rashomon set 'can guarantee that attacks do not transfer' (Section 1) is an overclaim relative to what is shown.

The stability results (Theorems 4, 5, 7) are largely expected consequences of loss boundedness and near-optimality definitions; Table 1's single-model vs. set-level contrast is more of a framing device than a substantive finding.

Originality is modest: non-transferability across diverse models, ensemble leakage, and stability of near-optimal sets under shifts are each intuitive and partially anticipated by prior work the paper itself cites (e.g., [20, 19, 42, 44, 45]); the synthesis is useful but the incremental depth is limited.
No released code or reproducibility artifacts are mentioned, and details such as dataset binarization choices and ε tuning (chosen to yield >100,000 trees) leave reproduction uncertain.

strengths: The paper addresses an underexplored and practically relevant question: how model multiplicity (the Rashomon set) jointly affects robustness, stability, and privacy, framing the Rashomon set as a 'policy object' rather than a theoretical curiosity. This framing is timely for trustworthy-ML governance.

The central thesis — a robustness–privacy trade-off induced by diversity — is supported from multiple angles: theoretical bounds (transferability via Hamming disagreement in Eq. (1), angular diversity for linear models in Thm 3/Corollaries 1-2, stability under distribution and dataset shifts in Thms 4-5, KL leakage bound in Thm 6) and consistent experiments across six real datasets (Figs. 3-5, 8-10).

The proofs (Appendices A-B) are correct as far as I can verify: the mutual information bound via Catalan-number counting (Thm 1), the Pinsker-based distribution-shift argument (Thm 4), the neighboring-dataset containment argument (Thm 5), and the finite-population sampling variance argument for the KL bound (Thm 6) are all sound.

The empirical verification of Theorem 5 (Fig. 10: Rashomon sets remain nested when tolerance is increased by 2K/n, and the controlled experiment with eps' = eps) is a particularly nice example of theory being validated quantitatively rather than only anecdotally.

The paper is commendably honest about scope: it clearly distinguishes distributional leakage from membership inference (Section 5.3), notes that Theorem 9's dependent-ensemble bound is 'not helpful', acknowledges that Adult and Bank show weaker diversity-robustness correlation, and states upfront that results are 'illustrative rather than exhaustive' (Table 1). Reproducibility is supported by detailed hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, and computation details (Appendix C).
weaknesses: The theoretical depth is modest. Several results are direct consequences of standard tools: Theorem 4 is essentially Pinsker's inequality applied to bounded losses, Theorem 5 follows from a trivial per-sample loss perturbation, Theorem 6 is the variance of a finite-population sample mean combined with a chi-squared bound on KL, and Theorem 3 is a direct computation of the margin shift. Eq. (1) is a one-line triangle inequality. The value lies in the framing and synthesis more than in novel technical machinery, which limits the contribution for a main-track theory standard.

The robustness evaluation is favorable to the claimed mechanism: the reported 'best adversarial accuracy among selected trees' (Sections 6.3, C.3) picks the most robust model after observing the attack, which presumes exactly the reactive model-switching capability the paper motivates but does not demonstrate in a deployment-like protocol (e.g., an adaptive attacker aware of the disclosed set, or a cost model for switching). The claim in the introduction that a diverse Rashomon set 'can guarantee that attacks do not transfer' is stronger than what the bounds (which require disagreement specifically on attacked points) support.

Some experimental design choices raise concern: the privacy (reconstruction) experiments use only 100 training samples per run, DRAFT is a reconstruction attack developed for random forests and applied here to Rashomon tree sets without validation that the attack remains near-optimal in this setting, and the main adversarial experiment uses an L-infinity attack with eta = 0.1 on binarized features (effectively a single feature flip), which is a weak adversary for demonstrating robustness gaps. The random baseline is also a very weak privacy comparator.

Support for the headline trade-off is uneven across datasets: Spearman correlations between diversity and adversarial robustness are only 0.23 (Adult) and 0.33 (Bank), and Figure 7 shows substantial scatter with zero-distance trees achieving high adversarial accuracy on those datasets. The paper attributes this to 'limited diversity' but offers no measurement or analysis of the proposed cause.

The KL-leakage story (Theorem 6, Fig. 2) is verified only on small synthetic distributions (d = 4, n = 100) and the bound depends on the population variance sigma^2(x), which itself measures disagreement; the connection between this distributional leakage and the concrete reconstruction attack used in Section 6.2 is asserted rather than formally linked.

Presentation issues: Theorem 9's title ('Dependent ensemble - this is not helpful') is informal and confusing; theorem ordering (Theorem 1 appears after Theorem 2 in Appendix A); notation such as n-bar+ is defined in a hard-to-parse way; and the R-S(eps)/R-hat_S(eps) notation is inconsistently typeset. These do not affect correctness but reduce polish.

Missing comparisons: there is no baseline showing how the reconstruction error or leakage compares to releasing, e.g., a single non-sparse model, a random forest of comparable aggregate capacity, or an explicitly differentially private ensemble, so the practical severity of the leakage increase from releasing 200 trees versus alternatives is hard to gauge.

strengths: The paper frames a coherent and useful question: treating the Rashomon set itself as the object of analysis for robustness, stability, and privacy, rather than optimizing individual trustworthiness criteria per model. This set-level perspective is well differentiated from closely related work (e.g., Hsu et al., 2026), and the robustness–privacy duality induced by model diversity is a genuinely interesting phenomenon.

The theoretical treatment is honest about its scope: reactive robustness is captured through a simple but clean disagreement bound (Eq. 1–2), linear-model results connect angular diversity to adversarial loss, and Theorems 5.4–5.6 correctly cover distribution-shift stability, neighborhood stability, and ensemble-based distributional leakage. The proofs in the appendix are complete and correct as far as I can verify.

The paper carefully and correctly distinguishes distributional leakage from membership privacy (Section 5.3), avoiding the common conflation of these notions, and honestly notes that the results do not claim robustness against all adaptive attacks.

The empirical work is broad: six tabular datasets, multiple sampling strategies (closest/farthest/increment/sparsity-based), reconstruction attacks via DRAFT, multi-model simultaneous attacks (Appendix E.3), stability verification of Theorem 5.5 (Appendix D.4), synthetic validation of Theorem 5.6 (Appendix D.5), and extensions to neural networks and Concept Bottleneck Models on AwA2, which supports generality beyond sparse trees.

The 'operationalization' section (Section 6.4, Appendix E.6) adds practical value by translating trade-off curves into disclosure guidance (knee points plus privacy floors), and the paper is clearly written with a helpful summary table (Table 2).
weaknesses: The theoretical results are largely elementary and largely assembled from standard tools: Theorem 4.1 is a coarse entropy/cardinality argument (I(f;S) ≤ H(f) ≤ O(l_f log d)) that conflates hypothesis-class size with actual leakage; Eqs. 1–2 are immediate triangle inequalities; Theorem 5.4 is a direct Pinsker application; Theorem 5.6 is a standard finite-population sampling variance calculation; Theorems C.6/C.7 are Chernoff and Cantelli bounds. While correct, the technical depth is modest for the main track.

The central empirical finding is partly mechanical: releasing more models from a Rashomon set necessarily gives an adversary a better ensemble approximation of the data, and the diversity–robustness correlation (Figure 2) can be partially tautological, since models similar to the attacked tree on clean data tend to agree with it on attacked points. The Spearman correlations also vary substantially (0.23 for Adult), and the authors' explanation (limited diversity) is only post-hoc.

The reconstruction experiments use only 100 training points (following Ferry et al., 2024), which inflates leakage magnitudes and limits the relevance to realistic disclosure scenarios. DRAFT was designed for random forests; its applicability and strength as an attack on deliberately diverse tree sets is not validated (e.g., against an adaptive attacker aware of the release strategy beyond the small E.3 study with only up to 10 trees via exponential search).

The claim that single sparse models are 'private' rests on the mutual-information lens and generalization-gap arguments; sparse trees can still leak via inversion in practice, and the paper does not empirically test single-model membership or inversion risk against the multi-model case on equal footing (the MIA experiments in Appendix E.5 show non-monotonic and weak effects, in tension with the stronger distributional-leakage story).

Some claims are under-supported: the 'sweet spot' privacy-first selection rule depends on arbitrary choices (δ = 0.35, Kneedle knee), and its framing as governance advice is speculative without validation on a real deployment or with regulators. Several proofs also carry strong assumptions (rule lists predicting majority labels, unit-norm weights in Corollary 5.2/5.3) whose practical restrictiveness is not always discussed.

Reproducibility is adequate on paper (datasets, hyperparameters, and compute are listed), but I did not see an explicit code release statement, and some experiments (e.g., TreeFARMS Rashomon sets with 100k–1.5M trees) may be costly to replicate.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and under-explored question: how model multiplicity (the Rashomon set), rather than a single deployed model, reshapes robustness, stability, and privacy. Framing the Rashomon set as a 'natural policy object' for governance is an interesting conceptual contribution.

The work combines theoretical results with experiments across multiple hypothesis spaces (rule lists, sparse decision trees, linear models, small MLPs, and Concept Bottleneck Models on images), which strengthens the generality of the qualitative claims.

The core mechanism for reactive robustness (Eq. 2, disagreement bounds adversarial loss differences) is clean and clearly explained, and the empirical trends (Spearman correlations between prediction-pattern distance and adversarial accuracy in Figure 6/7) are consistent with the theory.
The paper is clearly written, well organized, with a results summary table, thorough appendix with complete proofs, and empirical verification of each major theorem (Figures 5, 11, 16, 17).

The distinction between distributional leakage and membership privacy is handled carefully and honestly (Section 5.3), and the appendix discussion of sparsest-vs-densest strategies shows nuance rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: The theoretical results are largely shallow or standard. Theorem 4.1 is a counting/entropy bound; Theorem 5.4 is a direct application of Pinsker's inequality; Theorem 5.5 is a two-line triangle-inequality argument; Theorem 5.6 is a textbook finite-population sampling variance calculation; Theorems C.6/C.7 are Chernoff/Cantelli bounds. None of these yield tight, non-obvious, or technically demanding results, which limits the paper's technical depth for a main-track theory contribution.

The robustness-privacy 'trade-off' is largely constructed by the experimental design rather than being an intrinsic property. Reactive robustness is an internal property of a model pool and does not require disclosure; leakage only arises if models are released. The coupling of the two (a genuine trade-off) only holds under a specific disclosure scenario, and the paper does not clearly delineate when an institution that keeps the set internal faces any privacy cost at all.

The reactive robustness evaluation has an oracle-selection problem: the reported 'adversarial score' is the accuracy of the best-performing tree in the Rashomon set on the adversarial dataset (Sections 6.1, 6.3, E.5). In deployment, a practitioner cannot know which model is best under a future attack, so the numbers materially overstate achievable reactive robustness. A realistic rotation policy (e.g., random switching) should be evaluated instead.

The privacy experiments use a highly artificial threat model: Rashomon sets trained on only 100 data points, attacked with DRAFT, releasing up to 200 trees. Leakage on 100-sample training sets does not establish meaningful privacy risk at realistic data scales, and no comparison against a differential-privacy baseline or a quantitative leakage measure (e.g., epsilon estimates) is provided. The claim that 'sparse models are private' rests on an upper bound on mutual information (O(l log d)) that does not scale with n and therefore cannot distinguish a strongly overfit interpolating sparse model from a regularized one in any practically meaningful way.

Theorem 4.2 relies on strong assumptions (binary features, rules predicting majority labels, conjunctions of at most l literals) and its conclusion — that balanced datasets preclude robust rule lists under L0 attacks of size l+I−1 — is close to an observation that any low-margin classifier on separable-enough data is breakable with enough feature flips; the guaranteed-impact framing inflates its significance.

The neural network evidence is thin: the MLP experiments use toy datasets (Iris, Seeds, Wine with 2-layer, 8–16-unit networks) or AWP-approximated Rashomon sets, and the claim that trends 'extend to more complex architectures' is only weakly supported. The CBM experiment (Table 7) covers reactive robustness only, explicitly excluding the privacy side of the trade-off.

Reproducibility is not adequately addressed: no code or artifact release is mentioned, TreeFARMS parameters are partly tuned per dataset without a stated selection procedure, and the DRAFT/attack pipelines would be difficult to reimplement exactly from the manuscript alone.

The connection to prior work could be sharper: the observation that ensembles reveal more about the training distribution than individual models is closely related to known results on ensemble leakage and reconstruction attacks (e.g., the DRAFT line of work itself), and the incremental novelty over Hsu et al. (2026) — which the paper positions as per-model rather than set-level — needs to be argued more convincingly than the current related-work paragraph does.

strengths: Genuinely interesting and well-articulated framing: treating the Rashomon set as a 'policy object' and analyzing trustworthiness (robustness, privacy, stability) at the set level rather than the single-model level is a fresh and under-explored angle, clearly differentiated from per-model analyses like Hsu et al. (2026).

Comprehensive and well-designed empirical evaluation: six tabular datasets with TreeFARMS-enumerated Rashomon sets (100k+ trees), white-box adversarial attacks (Kantchelian et al.), dataset reconstruction via DRAFT, membership inference, multi-model simultaneous attacks, and extension to MLPs and Concept Bottleneck Models on AwA2 (Table 7).

Each theoretical claim is paired with an empirical verification (e.g., Theorem 5.5 verified in Fig. 11, Theorem 5.6 verified in Fig. 5, Theorem 4.2's vulnerability verified in Appendix E.2), which strengthens the soundness of the narrative.

Careful and honest discussion of scope: the paper explicitly distinguishes distributional leakage from membership privacy, acknowledges that diversity aligned with attack geometry is required for reactive robustness, and notes adaptive multi-model attack considerations (Appendix E.3).
Practical significance: the operationalization of the trade-off (Appendix E.6–E.8, knee/privacy-floor selection rule) offers a concrete starting point for disclosure policies in model governance.
Well written and well organized, with a results summary table and clear notation section.
weaknesses: The theoretical contributions are largely elementary: Eq. (1)–(2) are direct triangle inequalities; Theorem 5.4 is a standard Pinsker-based argument; Theorem 5.5 is a simple 2K/n empirical-risk perturbation bound; Theorem 5.6 is finite-population sampling theory (variance of the sample mean); Theorems C.6/C.7 are standard Chernoff/Cantelli bounds. The results are correct but their technical depth is modest for a main-track theory contribution.

Theorem 4.1 is loose and somewhat generic: I(f;S) ≤ H(f) ≤ log|F| applies to any hypothesis class of size |F|, so the 'sparsity ⇒ privacy' claim rests on a coarse counting argument; it does not establish meaningful privacy protection (and known model-inversion results on sparse linear models sit uneasily with the 'sparse models are private' framing).

The central robustness–privacy trade-off is an empirical observation rather than a formally derived result: the reactive-robustness bounds (Sec. 5.1) and the leakage bound (Thm 5.6) are developed separately and never combined into a quantitative trade-off relating diversity to both properties.

Reactive robustness assumes attacks target only the deployed optimal model; the adaptive multi-model threat is addressed only with a naive exponential-time search limited to 10 trees, which weakens the practical robustness claim against a realistic adversary who observes released models.

The privacy experiments rely on DRAFT, a reconstruction attack designed for random forests, applied to arbitrary Rashomon-set tree ensembles, and use only 100 training points, a setting that inflates reconstruction feasibility; the validity of reconstruction error as the leakage proxy in this context is asserted rather than validated.
The linear-model theory (Thm 5.1, Cors. 5.2–5.3) presumes a specific fixed attack direction (δ = −ηy ŵ/‖ŵ‖), limiting generality of the 'angle ⇒ robustness' conclusions.

No explicit code/artifact release is stated, which limits reproducibility of the multi-stage experimental pipeline (TreeFARMS enumeration, DRAFT integration, attack implementations) despite reliance on public datasets and tools.

Some findings (e.g., correlation between diversity and adversarial score) are largely confirmatory of the theory but the Adult/Bank Spearman coefficients (0.23, 0.33) are notably weaker, and the explanation (limited diversity) is speculative.
